habitat: Singly or in pairs in almost any non-forest habitat with trees.
summary: A common resident. A black drongo with a deep ruby-red eye, a powerful bill and a strongly forked tail, the outer feathers splayed. The sexes are alike. It gives unmusical twanging notes mixed with imitations, especially of owls and other birds of prey. The Kemp code RB was left unchanged.

similar.note: Common Square-tailed Drongo also has splayed outer tail feathers, but only a shallow fork. Fork-tailed Drongo has the deep fork.

population.notes: Kemp et al. 2001 order-of-magnitude threshold 2^17=131072 mature individuals (resident breeder); paper interval half–double → 65536–262144.

sources.title: Kemp A.C., Herholdt J.J., Whyte I. & Harrison J. (2001). Birds of the two largest national parks in South Africa: a method to generate estimates of population size for all species and assess their conservation ecology. S. Afr. J. Sci. 97: 393–403.

tail.shape: Deeply forked, the outer feathers splayed outwards.

viewNotes.note: Black, with a deep ruby-red eye and a strongly forked tail, the outer feathers splayed.
Black underparts and a ruby-red eye. The bill is powerful.
The deep fork shows from behind, with the outer feathers splayed.
Black above. A separate flight pattern was not described. It hawks from a perch.
Black below. The underside of the wing was not named.

calls.description: A variety of unmusical twanging notes, mixed with imitations of other birds, especially owls and birds of prey. Newman does not separate the sexes. Grade A call from Grahamstown. The filename is Fork-tailed drongo.mp3.

research.note: Status is resident and all twelve months are listed. Newman says the immature is as illustrated and gives no written plumage, so no immature variant was stored. Population figures were left unchanged.
